Chain of command, one line item each

WhoRoleFromToWhat they did
Dwight D. EisenhowerUS president19531961Managed early involvement: refused to bomb Dien Bien Phu (1954), backed Diem, sent military advisers — about 900 in country by the end of his term.
John F. KennedyUS president19611963Raised the adviser mission from under a thousand to about 16,000; approved the coup that removed Diem three weeks before his own assassination.
Lyndon B. JohnsonUS president19631969Oversaw the massive escalation: Gulf of Tonkin resolution (Aug 1964), Rolling Thunder (Mar 1965), first combat troops at Da Nang (Mar 1965), over 500,000 troops in country by 1968. Declined to run again after Tet.
Richard NixonUS president19691974Vietnamization: pulled US troops out while shifting the fighting to the South Vietnamese army; widened the air war to Cambodia and Laos; signed the Paris Peace Accords (Jan 1973). Last US combat troops left March 1973.
Gerald FordUS president19741977Asked Congress for aid to Saigon and was refused; ordered the evacuation. Saigon fell 30 April 1975.

Phases

1955–1964
Advisers

MAAG and then MACV train the ARVN; strategic hamlets; Buddhist crisis; Diem overthrown.

1965–1968
Escalation

Rolling Thunder; ground war of attrition under Westmoreland; search and destroy; Ia Drang, Khe Sanh, Tet (Jan 1968).

1969–1973
Vietnamization

Troop withdrawals; Cambodia incursion (1970); Lam Son 719 (1971); Easter Offensive and Linebacker (1972); Paris Accords (Jan 1973).

1973–1975
Collapse

Ceasefire ignored by both sides; US aid cut; Ho Chi Minh Campaign; fall of Saigon (30 Apr 1975).

Fit: 6 points from 1975-03-10, least squares, slope -0.69 per day, intercept 40.2.

The computer says zero on 1975-05-06. The ending, Fall of Saigon, was 1975-04-30. Error: 7 days late.

The model is a straight line through the provinces-held counts from Ban Me Thuot onward, extended to zero. It is late, not early: the line runs at the March pace, about one province a day, and the last fourteen provinces went in nine days once Xuan Loc fell. The difference between the computed date and 30 April is the speed of a collapse, which a line cannot see coming and which Weyand, on 4 April, could.

Cost

US military deaths58,220
ARVN military deaths~254,000
PAVN / Viet Cong deaths~1,100,000 (Vietnamese government figure)
Vietnamese civilian deathsestimates from ~600,000 to 2,000,000
US bomb tonnage, Indochina~7,500,000 tons, more than all of WWII
US cost~$168 billion then; roughly $1 trillion in 2020s dollars

Outcome

North Vietnamese victory; reunification under Hanoi (1976); US withdrawal complete two years before the end.

Open questions

  • Whether the Gulf of Tonkin second attack (4 Aug 1964) happened at all; the NSA's 2005 release says it did not.
  • Whether Kennedy would have withdrawn after 1964 (NSAM 263 vs. his public statements).
  • What Vietnamization was for: an exit, or a decent interval.
